chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Prince Andrew didn't just know he was going to die—he felt himself dying, already half gone. He was aware of a detachment from everything earthly, and a strange, joyful lightness filled him. Without hurry or anxiety, he waited for what was coming. That inexorable, eternal, distant, and unknown presence he had sensed throughout his entire life was now close to him, and through the strange lightness he felt, it had become almost understandable, almost something he could touch.
He had feared death before. Twice he had experienced that terrible, tormenting fear of the end—but now he no longer understood that fear.

The first time had been when the shell spun like a top in front of him, and he looked at the field, the bushes, and the sky, knowing he was face to face with death. When he came to himself after being wounded, a flower of eternal, unbound love had instantly opened in his soul, as if freed from the chains of life that had held it back. After that, he no longer feared death and stopped thinking about it.

During the hours of solitude, suffering, and partial delirium after his wound, the deeper he penetrated into this new principle of eternal love, the more he unconsciously detached himself from earthly life. To love everything and everyone, to always sacrifice oneself for love—that meant not loving anyone in particular, not living this earthly life. And the more he embraced that principle, the more he let go of life, and the more completely he dissolved the terrible barrier that—without such love—stands between life and death. When he first remembered he would have to die, he said to himself: "Well, so what? So much the better!"

But after that night in Mytishchi, when, half delirious, he had seen the woman he longed for appear before him, and pressing her hand to his lips had shed gentle, happy tears—love for one particular woman crept back unnoticed into his heart and bound him to life once more. Joyful, agitating thoughts began to fill his mind. Remembering the moment at the field hospital when he had seen Kuragin, he could no longer recapture what he had felt then, but was tormented by the question of whether Kuragin was still alive. And he didn't dare ask.

His illness followed its normal physical course, but what Natasha meant when she said "This suddenly happened" had occurred two days before Princess Mary arrived. It was the last spiritual struggle between life and death, in which death won. It was the unexpected realization that he still valued life—life as embodied in his love for Natasha—and a final, though ultimately defeated, attack of terror before the unknown.

It was evening. As usual after dinner, he was slightly feverish, and his thoughts were unusually clear. Sonya was sitting by the table. He began to doze off. Suddenly a feeling of happiness washed over him.
"Ah, she's here!" he thought.
And so she was: Natasha had come in silently and taken Sonya's place.

Ever since she had begun looking after him, he had always felt this physical awareness of her nearness. She sat in an armchair turned sideways, screening the candlelight from him, knitting a stocking. She had learned to knit after Prince Andrew casually mentioned that no one nurses the sick as well as old women who knit stockings, and that there's something soothing about it. The needles clicked lightly in her slender, quickly moving hands, and he could clearly see the thoughtful profile of her bowed face. She shifted, and the ball of yarn rolled off her knees. She started, glanced at him, and shielding the candle with her hand, stooped carefully with a smooth, precise movement, picked up the ball, and settled back into her former position.
He watched her without moving and saw that after bending down she wanted to take a deep breath but held back, breathing cautiously instead.

At the Troitsa monastery they had spoken of the past, and he had told her that if he survived, he would always thank God for his wound, which had brought them together again. But after that, they never spoke of the future.

"Can it be, or can it not?" he thought now, watching her and listening to the light click of the steel needles. "Could fate really have brought me to her so strangely only for me to die? Is it possible that the truth of life has been revealed to me only to show me that I've wasted my life in falsehood? I love her more than anything in the world! But what can I do if I love her?" He groaned involuntarily—a habit from his suffering.
Hearing that sound, Natasha put down the stocking, leaned closer, and suddenly noticing his shining eyes, stepped lightly to his side and bent over him.
"You're not asleep?"
"No, I've been watching you for a long time. I felt you come in. No one else gives me that sense of soft peace that you do... that light. I want to cry from joy."
Natasha moved closer to him. Her face shone with radiant happiness.
"Natasha, I love you too much! More than anything in the world."
"And I love you!"—she turned away for a moment. "Why too much?" she asked.
"Why too much?... Well, tell me—what do you feel in your soul, your whole soul—will I live? What do you think?"
"I'm sure of it, sure!" Natasha almost shouted, seizing both his hands with a passionate movement.
He was silent for a while.
"How wonderful that would be!" And taking her hand, he kissed it.
Natasha felt happy and stirred up, but immediately remembered that this wouldn't do—he needed to stay calm.
"But you haven't slept," she said, holding back her joy. "Try to sleep... please!"

He pressed her hand and let it go, and she went back to the candle and sat down again in her former position. Twice she turned to look at him, and her eyes met his, beaming at her. She set herself a goal on her stocking and resolved not to look around until she finished it.
Soon he really did close his eyes and fall asleep. He didn't sleep long and suddenly woke with a start, drenched in cold sweat.
As he fell asleep, he had still been thinking about the subject that now always occupied his mind—life and death, and mainly death. He felt himself closer to it.
"Love? What is love?" he thought.

"Love holds death back. Love is life. Everything I understand, I understand only because I love. Everything exists only because I love. Everything is united by love alone. Love is God, and to die means that I, a particle of love, will return to the universal, eternal source." These thoughts seemed comforting. But they were only thoughts. Something was missing—they weren't clear, they were too personal, too cerebral. And the old agitation and confusion remained. He fell asleep.

He dreamed he was lying in the room where he actually was, but perfectly well and unwounded. Various unimportant people appeared before him. He talked to them, discussed trivial things. They were getting ready to go somewhere. Prince Andrew vaguely realized that all this was trivial and that he had more important concerns, but he kept talking, surprising them with empty jokes. Gradually, unnoticed, all these people disappeared, and a single question—about the closed door—replaced everything else. He got up and went to bolt and lock the door. Everything depended on whether he could lock it in time. He tried to hurry, but his legs wouldn't move, and he knew he wouldn't make it. He was seized by an agonizing fear. That fear was the fear of death. It stood behind the door. But just as he was clumsily creeping toward it, that dreadful something on the other side was already pressing against it, forcing its way in. Something inhuman—death—was breaking through that door, and it had to be kept out. He grabbed the door, making a final effort to hold it back—locking it was no longer possible—but his efforts were weak and clumsy, and the door, pushed from behind by that terror, opened and closed again.
Once more it pushed from outside. His last superhuman efforts were useless, and both halves of the door swung silently open. It entered. It was death. And Prince Andrew died.
But at the very instant he died, Prince Andrew remembered that he was asleep, and at the very instant he died, making an effort, he woke up.

"Yes, that was death! I died—and woke up. Yes, death is an awakening!" And suddenly everything grew light in his soul, and the veil that had hidden the unknown was lifted from his inner vision. He felt as though powers that had been trapped within him were now released, and that strange lightness never left him again.
When he woke in a cold sweat and stirred on the couch, Natasha came to him and asked what was wrong. He didn't answer and looked at her strangely, without understanding.

That was what had happened two days before Princess Mary's arrival. From that day, as the doctor put it, the wasting fever turned malignant. But what the doctor said didn't concern Natasha—she could see the terrible spiritual symptoms that were far more convincing to her.

From that day onward, an awakening from life came to Prince Andrew alongside his awakening from sleep. And compared to the length of life, it didn't seem any slower to him than waking from sleep compared to the length of a dream.
There was nothing terrible or violent in this comparatively slow awakening.

His last days and hours passed in an ordinary, simple way. Both Princess Mary and Natasha, who never left him, felt this. They didn't weep or shudder, and during those final days they felt they were no longer tending to him—he was already gone—but to what most closely reminded them of him: his body. Both felt this so strongly that the outward, terrible side of death didn't touch them, and they didn't feel the need to feed their grief. They didn't cry in his presence or out of it, and they never talked to each other about him. They felt that no words could express what they understood.
They both watched him sinking slowly and quietly, deeper and deeper away from them, and they both knew it had to be this way, and that it was right.

He made his confession and received communion. Everyone came to say goodbye. When they brought his son to him, he pressed his lips to the boy's face and turned away—not because it was hard or sad (Princess Mary and Natasha understood that), but simply because he thought it was all that was required of him. When they told him to bless the boy, he did what was asked and looked around as if wondering whether there was anything else he should do.
When the last convulsions of the body, which the spirit was leaving, came, Princess Mary and Natasha were there.

"Is it over?" said Princess Mary, after his body had lain motionless for a few minutes, growing cold before them. Natasha went up, looked at the dead eyes, and hurried to close them. She closed them but didn't kiss them—instead she pressed herself against what reminded her most of him: his body.
"Where has he gone? Where is he now?..."
When the body, washed and dressed, lay in the coffin on a table, everyone came to say goodbye, and they all wept.

Little Nicholas cried because his heart was torn by painful confusion. The countess and Sonya cried from pity for Natasha and because he was gone. The old count cried because he felt that before long, he too would have to take that same terrible step.

Natasha and Princess Mary wept too, but not from personal grief. They wept with a reverent, softening emotion that had taken hold of their souls at the awareness of the simple, solemn mystery of death that had been accomplished in their presence.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: The human mind cannot grasp the causes of events in their totality, but the desire to find those causes is planted deep in the human soul. Without considering the countless complexity of conditions—any one of which, taken alone, might seem to be the cause—a person seizes on the first explanation that seems intelligible and says: 'This is the cause!' In historical events, the first and most primitive explanation was the will of the gods, and after that, the will of those who stood in the most prominent positions—the heroes of history. But we need only look beneath the surface of any historical event—which really lies in the activity of the masses who take part in it—to see that the will of the historical hero doesn't control the actions of the masses, but is itself constantly controlled. It may seem unimportant whether we understand historical events one way or another. Yet there is the same difference between someone who says 'the peoples of the West moved eastward because Napoleon wished it' and someone who says 'this happened because it had to happen,' as between those who believed the earth was stationary and the planets revolved around it, and those who admitted they didn't know what held the earth in place but knew there were laws governing its motion. There is, and can be, no cause of a historical event except the one cause of all causes. But there are laws directing events, and some of these laws we know while others we cannot yet comprehend. Discovering these laws becomes possible only when we completely abandon the attempt to find the cause in the will of any single individual, just as the laws of planetary motion were discovered only when people abandoned the idea that the earth was fixed.

Historians consider that, next to the Battle of Borodino and the occupation and burning of Moscow, the most important episode of the 1812 war was the movement of the Russian army from the Ryazan to the Kaluga road and to the Tarutino camp—the so-called flank march across the Krasnaya Pakhra River. They attribute this stroke of genius to various individuals and debate who deserves the credit. Even foreign historians, including the French, acknowledge the genius of the Russian commanders when they discuss this flank march. But it's hard to understand why military writers, and others following them, consider this maneuver to be some brilliant conception by a single man who saved Russia and destroyed Napoleon. First, it's hard to see where the genius lay, because it didn't take much brainpower to see that the best position for an army not under attack is where supplies are most plentiful—even a dull thirteen-year-old could have guessed that the best position after the retreat from Moscow was on the Kaluga road. So it's impossible to understand how historians conclude this was a profound maneuver. And it's even harder to understand why they think it saved Russia and destroyed the French, since this flank march—had it been preceded, accompanied, or followed by other circumstances—might have proved ruinous for the Russians. If the Russian army's position did begin to improve after this march, it doesn't follow at all that the march was the cause.

That flank march might not only have failed to benefit the Russian army but, under other circumstances, could have led to its destruction. What would have happened if Moscow hadn't burned down? If Murat hadn't lost sight of the Russians? If Napoleon hadn't remained inactive? If the Russian army at Krasnaya Pakhra had given battle, as Bennigsen and Barclay advised? What if the French had attacked the Russians while they were marching beyond the Pakhra? What if Napoleon had attacked the Russians approaching Tarutino with even a tenth of the energy he showed at Smolensk? What if the French had marched on Petersburg? In any of these scenarios, the flank march that supposedly brought salvation might have proved disastrous.

The third and most baffling thing is that historians studying this period deliberately avoid acknowledging that this flank march cannot be attributed to any single person, that no one foresaw it, and that in reality—like the retreat from Fili—it never occurred to anyone as a complete plan. It emerged moment by moment, step by step, event by event, from an endless number of diverse circumstances, and was only seen as a whole after it was accomplished and belonged to the past.

At the council at Fili, the prevailing idea among the Russian commanders was the most natural one: a direct retreat along the Nizhni road. Proof of this lies in the fact that the majority voted for such a retreat, and especially in the well-known conversation after the council between the commander in chief and Lanskoy, who was in charge of supplies. Lanskoy informed the commander in chief that army provisions were mostly stored along the Oka River in the Tula and Ryazan provinces, and that retreating toward Nizhni would separate the army from its supplies by the broad Oka, which can't be crossed early in winter. This was the first indication that they needed to deviate from the most natural course—a direct retreat toward Nizhni-Novgorod. The army turned more to the south, along the Ryazan road and closer to its supplies. Later, the French inactivity (they even lost sight of the Russian army), concern for the arsenal at Tula, and the advantage of moving closer to provisions caused the army to turn still further south onto the Tula road. After crossing to the Tula road beyond the Pakhra by a forced march, the Russian commanders planned to stay at Podolsk and had no thought of the Tarutino position. But countless circumstances—the reappearance of French troops, plans for giving battle, and above all the abundance of food in Kaluga province—forced the army to turn even further south, crossing from the Tula to the Kaluga road and proceeding to Tarutino, which lay between the supply routes. Just as it's impossible to say when the decision was made to abandon Moscow, it's impossible to say precisely when, or by whom, the decision was made to move to Tarutino. Only when the army had arrived there, as the result of innumerable and varying forces, did people begin assuring themselves that they had planned this movement all along and had foreseen its outcome.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 2
paragraphs: The famous flank movement was really quite simple: after the French advance had stopped, the Russian army—which had been retreating straight back from the invaders—veered away from that direct line and, finding it wasn't being pursued, naturally drifted toward the region where supplies were most plentiful.

If instead of imagining genius commanders leading the Russian army, we picture that army without any leaders at all, it couldn't have done anything but swing back toward Moscow in an arc toward the areas where food was most abundant and the land was richest.

This shift from the Nizhni toward the Ryazan, Tula, and Kaluga roads was so natural that even Russian marauders moved in that direction, and orders were sent from Petersburg for Kutuzov to take this very route. At Tarutino, Kutuzov received what amounted to a reprimand from the Emperor for moving along the Ryazan road, with the Emperor's letter pointing him toward the very position near Kaluga that he had already occupied.

Having rolled like a ball in the direction given by the momentum of the whole campaign and the Battle of Borodino, the Russian army—when that momentum was spent and no fresh push came—settled into its natural position.

Kutuzov's merit lay not in any so-called strategic masterstroke but in the fact that he alone understood the significance of what had happened. He alone grasped the meaning of the French army's inactivity. He alone continued to insist that the Battle of Borodino had been a victory. He alone—though as commander in chief he might have been expected to be eager to attack—used all his strength to hold the Russian army back from pointless engagements.

The beast wounded at Borodino was lying where the fleeing hunter had left it. Whether it was still alive, whether it was strong and merely lying low—the hunter didn't know. Suddenly the beast was heard to moan.
The moan of that wounded beast—the French army—which revealed its desperate condition, was the sending of Lauriston to Kutuzov's camp with peace proposals.
Napoleon, with his usual certainty that whatever entered his head was right, wrote to Kutuzov the first words that came to mind, though they meant nothing.

'My Prince Kutuzov: I am sending one of my adjutants-general to discuss several interesting questions with you. I beg Your Highness to believe what he says, especially when he expresses the sentiments of esteem and special regard I have long held for your person. This letter having no other purpose, I pray God to keep you in His holy and gracious protection!'
NAPOLEON
Moscow, October 30, 1812

Kutuzov replied: 'I would be cursed by future generations if I were seen as the one who initiated any kind of settlement. Such is the spirit of my nation.' But he continued to use all his powers to keep his troops from attacking.

During the month the French troops spent looting Moscow while the Russian troops rested quietly at Tarutino, a shift had taken place in the relative strength of the two armies—both in spirit and in numbers—so that the advantage had passed to the Russian side. Although the Russians didn't know the exact condition and numbers of the French army, as soon as this shift occurred, the need to attack became obvious through countless signs: Lauriston's mission, the abundance of supplies at Tarutino, the reports pouring in from all sides about French disorder and inactivity, the flow of recruits into Russian regiments, the fine weather, the long rest the Russian soldiers had enjoyed, and the natural impatience to do what they'd been assembled for, which usually shows itself in an army that has been resting, curiosity about what the French army, so long out of sight, was doing, the boldness of Russian outposts scouting close to the French positions at Tarutino, news of easy victories by peasants and guerrillas, the envy this aroused, the desire for revenge that burned in every Russian heart while the French remained in Moscow, and above all a dim awareness in every soldier's mind that the balance of power had shifted and the advantage was now theirs. A real change had occurred, and an advance had become inevitable. And at once—just as a clock begins to strike and chime when the minute hand completes its circle—this change showed itself through increased activity, buzzing, and ringing in the higher command.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: The Russian army was being commanded by Kutuzov and his staff, and also by the Emperor from Petersburg. Before news of the abandonment of Moscow had reached Petersburg, a detailed plan for the entire campaign had been drawn up and sent to Kutuzov for guidance. Though this plan assumed Moscow was still in Russian hands, it was approved by the staff and accepted as the basis for action. Kutuzov replied only that plans made at a distance were always difficult to execute. So fresh instructions were sent for handling difficulties that might arise, along with new people to watch Kutuzov's actions and report on them.

Beyond this, the entire Russian army staff was being reorganized. The positions left vacant by Bagration, who had been killed, and by Barclay, who had departed in a huff, had to be filled. Very serious thought was given to whether it would be better to put A in B's place and B in D's, or the reverse—as if anything beyond A's or B's personal satisfaction depended on these decisions.

As a result of the hostility between Kutuzov and Bennigsen (his chief of staff), the presence of the Emperor's confidential representatives, and all these personnel changes, an unusually complicated web of political maneuvering was underway among the staff. A was undermining B, D was undermining C, and so on in every possible combination. In all these intrigues, the subject was supposedly the conduct of the war, which everyone believed they were directing. But the war went on independently of them all, following its own course—never the way people planned it, but flowing always from the essential attitude of the masses. Only in the highest circles did all these schemes and machinations appear to reflect what actually had to happen.

"Prince Michael Ilarionovich!" wrote the Emperor on the second of October, in a letter that reached Kutuzov after the battle of Tarutino. "Since September 2, Moscow has been in enemy hands. Your last reports were dated the twentieth, and since then no action has been taken against the enemy or to relieve the ancient capital. According to your latest dispatch, you have even retreated further. Serpukhov is already occupied by an enemy detachment, and Tula with its famous arsenal, so vital to the army, is in danger. From General Wintzingerode's reports, I see that an enemy corps of ten thousand is moving on the Petersburg road. Another of several thousand moves on Dmitrov. A third has advanced along the Vladimir road, and a fourth, quite sizable, is stationed between Ruza and Mozhaysk. Napoleon himself was in Moscow as late as the twenty-fifth. Given all this, when the enemy has scattered his forces into large detachments and Napoleon sits in Moscow with his Guards, is it really possible that the forces facing you are too strong for you to take the offensive? On the contrary, he is probably only chasing you with detachments, or at most with a corps far weaker than your army. It would seem you could advantageously attack a weaker force and destroy it, or at least force it to retreat, holding an important part of the provinces now under enemy control and averting the danger to Tula and other interior towns. You will be held responsible if the enemy manages to direct a significant force against Petersburg, where we have been unable to keep many troops. With the army entrusted to you, acting with resolution and energy, you have ample means to prevent this fresh disaster. Remember that you still must answer to our offended country for the loss of Moscow. You have seen my readiness to reward you. That readiness will not weaken, but I and Russia have a right to expect from you all the zeal, firmness, and success that your intellect, military talent, and the courage of your troops justify us in expecting."

But by the time this letter—which showed that the real balance of forces had already made itself felt even in Petersburg—was sent, Kutuzov had found himself unable to hold back his army any longer, and a battle had already taken place.

On October second, a Cossack named Shapovalov, who was out scouting, killed one hare and wounded another. Following the wounded hare, he wandered deep into the forest and stumbled upon the left flank of Murat's army, camped there without any precautions. The Cossack laughingly told his comrades how he'd nearly fallen into French hands. A junior officer, hearing the story, passed it to his commander.

The Cossack was brought in and questioned. The Cossack officers wanted to seize the chance to capture some horses, but one of the senior officers, who had connections to the higher authorities, reported the incident to a general on the staff. Things at staff headquarters had been extremely tense lately. Ermolov had recently visited Bennigsen and begged him to use his influence to persuade the commander in chief to take the offensive.
"If I didn't know you, I'd think you didn't actually want what you're asking for. I only have to suggest something for His Highness to do the opposite," Bennigsen replied.

The Cossack's report, confirmed by cavalry patrols sent out afterward, was the final proof that events had ripened. The tightly coiled spring was released, the clock began to whir and the chimes to play. Despite all his supposed power, his intellect, his experience, and his knowledge of men, Kutuzov—taking into account the Cossack's report, Bennigsen's note to the Emperor, the wishes he assumed the Emperor held, and the unanimous desire of all his generals—could no longer hold back the inevitable. He gave the order to do what he considered useless and harmful—he approved, that is, the accomplished fact.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Bennigsen's note and the Cossack's report about the unguarded French left flank were merely the final signs that an attack was necessary. It was set for October fifth.
On the morning of the fourth, Kutuzov signed the battle orders. Toll read them to Ermolov, asking him to handle the further arrangements.
"Fine, fine. I don't have time right now," Ermolov replied, and left the hut.
The orders drawn up by Toll were quite good. Just as with the Austerlitz orders, though not in German this time, it was written:

"The First Column will march here and here," "the Second Column will march there and there," and so on. On paper, all these columns arrived at their positions on time and destroyed the enemy. Everything had been admirably planned, as is always the case with battle orders—and as is always the case, not a single column reached its position on time.

When enough copies of the orders had been prepared, an officer was called to deliver them to Ermolov. A young officer of the Horse Guards, Kutuzov's orderly, was pleased with the importance of his mission and set off for Ermolov's quarters.
"He's gone out," said Ermolov's orderly.
The Horse Guards officer went to a general with whom Ermolov was often found.
"No, and the general's out too."
The officer mounted his horse and rode to someone else.
"No, he's gone out."

"If they blame me for this delay! What a nuisance!" thought the officer, and he rode around the entire camp. One person said he'd seen Ermolov ride by with other generals; others said he must have gone home. The officer searched until six in the evening without stopping to eat. Ermolov was nowhere to be found, and no one knew where he was. The officer grabbed a quick meal at a comrade's place and rode to the vanguard to find Miloradovich. Miloradovich was also away, but there they told him he'd gone to a ball at General Kikin's, and that Ermolov was probably there too.
"But where is it?"
"Over there, at Echkino," said a Cossack officer, pointing to a country house in the far distance.
"What—outside our lines?"
"They've posted two regiments as outposts, and they're having quite a party in there. It's something else! Two bands and three groups of singers!"
The officer rode beyond the Russian lines to Echkino. While still far off, he could hear the merry sounds of a soldier's dance song coming from the house.

"In the meadows... in the meadows!" came the singing, accompanied by whistling and the twang of a stringed instrument, drowned now and then by shouts. The sounds lifted his spirits, but at the same time he feared being blamed for not delivering his important orders sooner. It was already past eight o'clock. He dismounted and walked up to the porch of a large country house that had somehow survived intact between the Russian and French positions. In the refreshment room and the hall, servants bustled about with wine and food. Groups of singers stood outside the windows. The officer was admitted and immediately saw all the senior generals of the army gathered together, including Ermolov's big, imposing figure. They all had their coats unbuttoned and stood in a semicircle, their faces flushed and animated, laughing loudly. In the middle of the room, a short, handsome general with a red face was dancing the trepak with tremendous energy and skill.
"Ha, ha, ha! Bravo, Nicholas Ivanych! Ha, ha, ha!"

The officer felt that arriving with important orders at such a moment made him doubly guilty. He would have preferred to wait, but one of the generals spotted him and, hearing what he'd come about, informed Ermolov.
Ermolov came forward frowning and, hearing the officer's report, took the papers without a word.

"You think he went off by chance?" a comrade on the staff said to the Horse Guards officer that evening, referring to Ermolov. "It was a trick. It was done on purpose to get Konovnitsyn in trouble. You'll see what a mess there'll be tomorrow."

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The next day, the aging Kutuzov got up early, said his prayers, dressed, and with the unpleasant awareness of having to direct a battle he didn't approve of, climbed into his carriage and drove from Letashovka—a village three and a half miles from Tarutino—to where the attacking columns were supposed to assemble. He sat in the carriage, dozing and waking by turns, listening for any sound of gunfire on the right that would signal the action had begun. But everything was still quiet. A damp, gray autumn morning was just dawning. Approaching Tarutino, Kutuzov noticed cavalrymen leading their horses to water across the road he was driving along. He studied them closely, stopped his carriage, and asked what regiment they belonged to. They were part of a column that should have been far ahead, already in ambush position long before. 'Maybe it's a mistake,' thought the old commander in chief. But a little farther on, he saw infantry regiments with their weapons stacked, soldiers half-dressed, eating porridge and gathering firewood. He sent for an officer. The officer reported that no order to advance had been received.

'What! Not rec—' Kutuzov began, but caught himself and sent for a senior officer. Getting out of his carriage, he stood with his head drooping, breathing heavily, pacing silently up and down. When Eykhen, the staff officer he'd summoned, appeared, Kutuzov turned purple in the face—not because Eykhen was to blame, but because he was a sufficiently important target for his fury. Trembling and gasping, the old man fell into one of those rages in which he sometimes used to roll on the ground. He fell on Eykhen, shaking his fists, shouting and heaping vile abuse on him. Another officer, Captain Brozin, who happened to appear and was not at all to blame, suffered the same fate.
'What kind of scoundrel are you? I'll have you shot! Blackguards!' Kutuzov yelled in a hoarse voice, waving his arms and staggering.

He was suffering physically. He—the commander in chief, a Serene Highness whom everyone said held powers no man in Russia had ever possessed—to be put in this position, made the laughingstock of the whole army! 'I needn't have rushed to pray this morning, or stayed up all night thinking everything through,' he thought. 'When I was a young officer, no one would have dared mock me like this... and now!' He was in a state of physical anguish, as if he'd been beaten, and couldn't help expressing it through cries of anger and distress. But his strength soon gave out. Looking around, conscious of having said too much, he climbed back into his carriage and drove away in silence.

His rage, once spent, didn't return. Blinking wearily, he listened to excuses and justifications (Ermolov didn't come to see him until the next day) and to the insistence of Bennigsen, Konovnitsyn, and Toll that the failed operation should be attempted again the following day. Once more, Kutuzov had to consent.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: The next day, the troops assembled at their positions in the evening and advanced during the night. It was an autumn night with dark purple clouds but no rain. The ground was damp but not muddy, and the troops moved forward silently—only the occasional clinking of artillery could be faintly heard. The men were forbidden to talk aloud, smoke their pipes, or strike a light, and they tried to keep their horses from neighing. The secrecy heightened the adventure's appeal, and they marched cheerfully. Some columns, thinking they'd reached their destination, halted, stacked arms, and settled on the cold ground, but the majority marched all night and ended up in the wrong places.

Only Count Orlov-Denisov with his Cossacks—the least important detachment of all—reached his appointed position on time. His detachment halted at the edge of a forest on the path from the village of Stromilova to Dmitrovsk.

Toward dawn, Count Orlov-Denisov, who had dozed off, was woken by a French deserter being brought to him. It was a Polish sergeant from Poniatowski's corps who explained in Polish that he'd deserted because he'd been overlooked for promotion: he should have been made an officer long ago, he was braver than any of them, and so he'd left to pay them back. He said Murat was spending the night less than a mile away, and if they gave him a hundred men, he'd capture him alive. Count Orlov-Denisov consulted his fellow officers.

The offer was too tempting to refuse. Everyone volunteered, and everyone advised making the attempt. After much debate, Major-General Grekov set off with two Cossack regiments and the Polish sergeant.
"Now remember," Count Orlov-Denisov said to the sergeant as he left, "if you've been lying, I'll hang you like a dog. But if it's true, you'll get a hundred gold coins."

The sergeant, without a word, mounted up with a resolute air and rode off with Grekov, whose men had quickly assembled. They vanished into the forest. Count Orlov-Denisov, having seen them off, returned, shivering in the freshness of early dawn and excited by what he'd taken on. He began scanning the enemy camp, now just visible in the deceptive predawn light and the dying campfires. The Russian columns should have been appearing on the open slope to his right. He looked that way, but though the columns would have been visible from quite far off, they were nowhere to be seen. It seemed to the count that something was stirring in the French camp, and his sharp-eyed adjutant confirmed this.
"Oh, it's really too late," said Count Orlov, looking at the camp.

As often happens when someone you trusted is no longer in front of you, it suddenly seemed perfectly clear to him that the sergeant was a fraud, that he'd lied, and that the whole Russian attack would be ruined by the absence of those two regiments he'd sent off to God knows where. How could anyone capture a commander in chief from the middle of such a mass of troops!
"I'm sure that scoundrel was lying," said the count.
"They can still be called back," said one of his officers, who felt the same distrust as he looked at the enemy camp.
"Well? Really... what do you think? Should we let them go on or not?"
"Should I have them called back?"
"Call them back, call them back!" said Count Orlov with sudden decisiveness, looking at his watch. "It'll be too late. It's getting light."

The adjutant galloped through the forest after Grekov. When Grekov returned, Count Orlov-Denisov—stirred up by the abandoned attempt, frustrated by the infantry columns that still hadn't appeared, and energized by the enemy's nearness—decided to attack anyway. All his men felt the same excitement.
"Mount!" he commanded in a whisper. The men took their positions and crossed themselves. "Forward, with God's help!"
"Hurrah!" echoed through the forest, and the Cossack companies, lances trailing, poured out one after another like grain from a sack and dashed merrily across the stream toward the camp.

One desperate, terrified shriek from the first French soldier who spotted the Cossacks, and everyone in the camp—undressed, barely awake—scattered in all directions, abandoning cannons, muskets, and horses.

If the Cossacks had pursued the French without worrying about what was behind and around them, they could have captured Murat and everything else. That was what the officers wanted. But it was impossible to budge the Cossacks once they had their hands on loot and prisoners. None of them listened to orders. Fifteen hundred prisoners and thirty-eight guns were taken on the spot, along with standards and—what mattered most to the Cossacks—horses, saddles, horse blankets, and the like. All this had to be dealt with: the prisoners secured, the guns claimed, the booty divided—not without some shouting and even a bit of fighting among themselves—and this was what kept the Cossacks busy.
The French, no longer being pursued, began to regroup and opened fire. Orlov-Denisov, still waiting for the other columns, advanced no further.

Meanwhile, according to the orders that said "the First Column will march" and so on, the infantry of the late-arriving columns—commanded by Bennigsen and directed by Toll—had started out properly but, as always happens, ended up somewhere, just not where they were supposed to be. As always, the men set out cheerfully, then began to halt; grumbling was heard, confusion set in, and finally they started moving backward. Adjutants and generals galloped about, shouted, grew angry, quarreled, said they'd gone completely wrong and were late, vented their frustration, and finally gave up trying to follow the plan and just marched forward. "We'll end up somewhere!" And they did end up somewhere, just not in the right places. A few eventually did reach their designated positions, but too late to be useful—just in time to be shot at. Toll, who played the same role in this battle as Weyrother had at Austerlitz, galloped tirelessly from place to place, finding everything in chaos everywhere. He stumbled upon Bagovut's corps in a wood when it was already broad daylight, though it should have joined Orlov-Denisov long before. Furious about the failure, assuming someone must be responsible, Toll galloped up to the corps commander and began berating him savagely, saying he ought to be shot. General Bagovut—a veteran soldier of calm temperament—was also upset by all the delays, confusion, and crossed purposes, and to everyone's surprise flew into a rage completely out of character, saying unpleasant things to Toll.
"I don't need lessons from anyone, but I can die with my men as well as anybody," he said, and advanced with a single division.

Coming out into the open under enemy fire, this brave general marched straight ahead, leading his men into battle without considering, in his anger, whether attacking now with a single division would serve any purpose at all. The danger, the cannonballs, the bullets—that was exactly what he needed in his furious state. One of the first bullets killed him, and others killed many of his men. His division remained under fire for some time, entirely uselessly.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Meanwhile, another column was supposed to attack the French from the front, but Kutuzov accompanied it. He knew perfectly well that nothing but chaos would come of this battle fought against his will, and as far as he could, he held the troops back. He did not advance.
He rode silently on his small gray horse, lazily brushing off suggestions that they should attack.
"You always want to attack, but you don't see that we're incapable of carrying out complicated maneuvers," he said to Miloradovich, who asked permission to advance.
"We couldn't capture Murat this morning or get to our positions in time, and nothing can be done now!" he told someone else.

When Kutuzov was informed that behind the French rear—where, according to the Cossacks' reports, there had been nobody before—two Polish battalions had now appeared, he shot a sidelong glance at Ermolov, who was behind him and to whom he hadn't spoken since the day before.
"You see! They keep asking to attack and making all kinds of plans, but as soon as it comes to action, nothing is ready, and the enemy, forewarned, takes countermeasures."
Ermolov narrowed his eyes and smiled faintly at these words. He understood that the storm had passed for him, and that Kutuzov would be satisfied with just this hint.
"He's having a little fun at my expense," Ermolov said quietly, nudging Raevsky with his knee.
Shortly after, Ermolov approached Kutuzov and remarked respectfully:
"It's not too late yet, Your Highness—the enemy hasn't pulled back. If you would order an attack... Otherwise the Guards won't even get a glimpse of smoke."
Kutuzov didn't respond, but when they reported that Murat's troops were retreating, he ordered an advance—though he halted for three-quarters of an hour at every hundred paces.
The entire battle amounted to what Orlov-Denisov's Cossacks had accomplished. The rest of the army simply lost a few hundred men for nothing.

As a result of this battle, Kutuzov received a diamond decoration, Bennigsen received diamonds and a hundred thousand rubles, and others received pleasant rewards according to their rank. After the battle, fresh staff changes were made.

"That's how everything is done with us—all upside down!" said the Russian officers and generals after the Battle of Tarutino, suggesting that some fool had done things all wrong but that they themselves would never have blundered so—just as people talk today. But those who say such things either don't know what they're talking about or are deliberately fooling themselves. No battle—Tarutino, Borodino, or Austerlitz—ever goes as its planners expected. That is a fundamental truth.

A countless number of free forces (for nowhere is a man freer than in battle, where life and death hang in the balance) shape the course of a fight, and that course can never be known in advance and never coincides with any single force's direction.

If many forces act simultaneously on a body from different directions, the resulting movement cannot coincide with any one of them but will always be an average—what mechanics represents as the diagonal of a parallelogram of forces.
If we find in historians' accounts—especially French ones—that their wars and battles went according to prearranged plans, the only conclusion we can draw is that those accounts are false.

The Battle of Tarutino clearly didn't achieve Toll's aim of leading the troops into action according to the dispositions; nor Count Orlov-Denisov's possible aim of capturing Murat; nor Bennigsen's goal of immediately destroying the entire corps; nor the ambitions of the officer eager to distinguish himself; nor the Cossack's wish for more loot. But if the aim of the battle was what actually resulted and what all Russians desired—to drive the French out of Russia and destroy their army—then it's quite clear that the Battle of Tarutino, precisely because of its confusion, was exactly what was needed at that stage of the campaign. It would be difficult, even impossible, to imagine a better outcome. With minimal effort and insignificant losses, despite the greatest disorder, the most important results of the entire campaign were achieved: the transition from retreat to advance, the exposure of French weakness, and the delivery of that shock Napoleon's army had been waiting for to begin its flight.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: Napoleon enters Moscow after the brilliant victory at the Moskva; the victory is beyond doubt, since the battlefield remains in French hands. The Russians retreat and abandon their ancient capital. Moscow, overflowing with provisions, weapons, ammunition, and incalculable wealth, is in Napoleon's hands. The Russian army, only half the strength of the French, doesn't make a single attempt to attack for an entire month. Napoleon's position is magnificent. He can either fall on the Russian army with double their strength and destroy it; negotiate a favorable peace; or, if refused, make a threatening move on Petersburg; or even, in case of a setback, fall back to Smolensk or Vilna; or simply stay in Moscow. In short, no special genius would seem necessary to hold the brilliant position the French occupied at that time. All that was needed were very simple, obvious steps: don't let the troops loot, prepare winter clothing (there was enough in Moscow for the whole army), and systematically collect the provisions which, according to French historians, were sufficient to supply the army for six months. Yet Napoleon—that greatest of all geniuses, who historians claim controlled the army—took none of these steps.

Not only did he fail to do any of this, but he used his power to choose the most foolish and ruinous of all available options. Of everything Napoleon might have done—wintering in Moscow, marching on Petersburg or Nizhni-Novgorod, or retreating by a northern or southern route (say, the road Kutuzov later took)—nothing more stupid or disastrous can be imagined than what he actually did. He lingered in Moscow until October, letting the troops plunder the city. Then, hesitating whether to leave a garrison behind, he abandoned Moscow, approached Kutuzov without giving battle, veered right and reached Malo-Yaroslavets, again without trying to break through and take Kutuzov's road, and instead retreated to Mozhaysk along the devastated Smolensk road. Nothing more idiotic could have been devised—or more devastating for the army, as events soon proved. If Napoleon's goal had been to destroy his own army, the most brilliant strategist could hardly have come up with a series of actions that would accomplish it more completely, regardless of anything the Russian army might do.

Napoleon, the man of genius, did this. But to say he destroyed his army because he wanted to, or because he was very stupid, would be as unjust as saying he had brought his troops to Moscow because he wanted to and because he was very clever.
In both cases, his personal actions—having no more force than any individual soldier's—merely coincided with the laws that governed the events.

Historians quite falsely portray Napoleon's abilities as having weakened in Moscow, and they do this only because the results didn't justify his actions. He applied all his skill and strength to do the best he could for himself and his army, just as he had done before and would do again in 1813. His activity during this period was no less remarkable than in Egypt, Italy, Austria, or Prussia. We can't be certain how genuine his genius was in Egypt—where forty centuries looked down on his glory—since the accounts come entirely from the French. We can't accurately assess his genius in Austria or Prussia either, since our information comes from French or German sources, and the mysterious surrender of entire corps and fortresses without a fight naturally inclines Germans to credit his genius as the only explanation. But we, thank God, don't need to invoke his genius to cover up our shame. We have earned the right to look at this matter plainly and simply, and we won't give up that right.

His activity in Moscow was as remarkable and as full of genius as anywhere else. Order after order and plan after plan poured from him, from the moment he entered Moscow until the moment he left. The absence of citizens and a deputation, and even the burning of Moscow, didn't faze him. He never lost sight of his army's welfare, the enemy's movements, the welfare of the Russian people, the direction of affairs in Paris, or the diplomatic considerations surrounding the anticipated peace.

chapters.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: Regarding military matters, Napoleon immediately upon entering Moscow gave General Sebastiani strict orders to monitor the Russian army's movements, sent army corps along the various roads, and instructed Murat to find Kutuzov. Then he carefully oversaw the fortification of the Kremlin and drew up a brilliant plan for a future campaign covering the entire map of Russia.

In diplomatic affairs, Napoleon summoned Captain Yakovlev—who had been robbed, was dressed in rags, and had no idea how to get out of Moscow—and explained his entire policy and his magnanimity in great detail. Having written a letter to Emperor Alexander in which he felt duty-bound to inform his Friend and Brother that Rostopchin had badly mismanaged things in Moscow, he dispatched Yakovlev to Petersburg.
Having similarly explained his views and his magnanimity to Tutolmin, he sent that old man off to Petersburg to negotiate as well.
In legal matters, immediately after the fires, he ordered that the arsonists be found and executed. And the 'scoundrel' Rostopchin was punished by an order to burn down his houses.
In administrative affairs, Moscow was granted a constitution. A municipal government was established and the following announcement issued:
CITIZENS OF MOSCOW!

Your misfortunes are terrible, but His Majesty the Emperor and King wishes to end them. Harsh examples have shown you how he punishes disobedience and crime. Strict measures have been taken to restore order and public safety. A fatherly administration, chosen from among yourselves, will form your municipal government. It will care for you, your needs, and your welfare. Its members will be marked by a red ribbon worn across the shoulder, and the mayor will also wear a white belt. But when not on duty, they will wear only a red ribbon on the left arm.

The city police has been restored on its former basis, and its activity has already improved public order. The government has appointed two commissaries general, or police chiefs, and twenty ward commissioners to the city's different districts. You will know them by the white ribbon on their left arm. Several churches of various denominations are open, and services continue without interference. Your fellow citizens are returning daily, and orders have been given that they shall find help and protection in their homes. These are the government's measures to restore order and ease your condition. But to achieve this, you must add your own efforts: forget, if possible, the misfortunes you've suffered; trust in a less cruel fate; be certain that inevitable, shameful death awaits anyone who threatens your persons or your remaining property; and have no doubt that your safety is assured, for such is the will of the greatest and most just of monarchs. Soldiers and citizens, whatever your nation—restore public trust, the foundation of a state's welfare. Live as brothers, give each other aid and protection, unite to resist the evil-minded, obey the military and civil authorities, and your tears will soon dry!
Regarding army provisions, Napoleon decreed that all troops should take turns entering Moscow to forage—'à la maraude' *—so the army could provide for itself.
* As looters.
Regarding religion, Napoleon ordered the priests brought back and services resumed in the churches.
Regarding trade and army supplies, the following was posted everywhere:
PROCLAMATION

You, peaceful citizens of Moscow, artisans and workers driven from the city by misfortune, and you scattered farmers still kept from your fields by groundless fear—listen! Peace is returning to this capital and order is being restored. Your countrymen are emerging boldly from hiding, finding they are treated with respect. Any violence to them or their property is promptly punished. His Majesty the Emperor and King protects them and considers none of you his enemy except those who disobey his orders. He wishes to end your suffering and return you to your homes and families. Come to us without fear. Citizens, return confidently to your dwellings! You will soon find ways to meet your needs. Craftsmen and industrious workers, return to your trades, your homes, your shops, where guards await to protect you! You will receive proper pay for your work. And you, peasants—come out of the forests where you hide in terror. Return to your villages without fear, knowing you will find protection! Markets have been set up in the city where you may bring your surplus produce. The government has ensured free trade through the following measures: (1) Starting today, farmers and those living near Moscow may safely bring supplies of all kinds to two designated markets—one on Mokhovaya Street and the other at the Provision Market. (2) Goods will be purchased at prices agreed between buyer and seller, and if a seller cannot get a fair price, he may freely take his goods home—no one may hinder him. (3) Sundays and Wednesdays are the main market days, with sufficient troops stationed along the highways on Tuesdays and Saturdays to protect supply carts. (4) Similar measures will protect peasants returning with their carts. (5) Steps will be taken immediately to restore normal trade.

Citizens and villagers, workers and artisans of all nations—you are called to carry out the fatherly intentions of His Majesty the Emperor and King and to work with him for the common good! Place your trust at his feet and join us without delay!

To raise the spirits of both troops and civilians, reviews were constantly held and rewards distributed. The Emperor rode through the streets to comfort the residents and, despite his preoccupation with state affairs, personally attended the theaters he had ordered to be set up.

In matters of philanthropy—the supreme virtue of crowned heads—Napoleon did everything in his power. He had the words 'House of My Mother' inscribed on charitable institutions, blending tender filial devotion with a monarch's majestic generosity. He visited the Foundling Hospital and, allowing the orphans he had 'saved' to kiss his white hands, conversed graciously with Tutolmin. Then, as Thiers eloquently recounts, he ordered his soldiers to be paid in forged Russian currency he had prepared: 'Ennobling the use of these means by an act worthy of himself and of the French army, he had relief distributed to fire victims. But as food was too precious to give to foreigners—most of whom were enemies—Napoleon preferred to supply them with money to buy food from outside, and had paper rubles distributed to them.'
Regarding military discipline, orders were continually issued imposing severe punishment for neglect of duty and to suppress looting.
